rationale: The hypothesis that cerebellar ataxia is present in 85% (approximately 38/45) of patients with biallelic ACBD6 mutations and is associated with gait impairment in 94% of cases is directly supported by the landmark clinical cohort study by Kaiyrzhanov et al. (2024), which evaluated 45 affected individuals across 28 unrelated families. Secondary literature in movement disorders also confirms gait ataxia and dystonia as defining phenotypic features pointing to recessive ACBD6 mutations, with no contradicting cohorts or refuting reports identified in the literature.

evidence.text: In a cohort of 45 individuals from 28 unrelated families with bi-allelic pathogenic ACBD6 variants, mild cerebellar ataxia was documented in 85% of patients, and gait impairment was reported in 94% of cases, co-occurring alongside other movement abnormalities such as dystonia (94%) and spasticity (76%).

evidence.text: A meta-synthesis of hyperkinetic disorders in neurodevelopmental syndromes identified that the specific clinical presentation of gait ataxia together with corpus callosum abnormalities/agenesis and axial dystonia strongly points toward recessive ACBD6 mutations.

new_directions.question_text: To what degree is cerebellar ataxia clinically masked or underdiagnosed when severe lower limb spasticity (76%) or generalized dystonia (94%) dominates the motor presentation in older ACBD6 patients?
new_directions.rationale: Kaiyrzhanov et al. observed progressive postural deformities and parkinsonism with advancing age, which could hinder formal assessment of appendicular or truncal cerebellar ataxia over time.
